d.title: Three properties, each breaking a different testing assumption
d.caption: **Non-determinism** breaks the idea that a test has an outcome — temperature above zero gives different output each run, and 1.7 measured that even at zero the provider's batching moves the logits. **Open-endedness** breaks exact match, because many valid answers exist and no single correct string does. And **multi-dimensionality** breaks the single number: an answer can be correct but unsafe, or helpful but ungrounded, and one score cannot say which.

cells.text: the idea that a test has one outcome
exact match - there is no single correct string
the single number - correct but unsafe is a real state

d.title: Four rungs, and human eval's real job
d.caption: The ladder runs from free to expensive, and the last row's *use for* column is the one worth reading: **human evaluation's primary job is calibrating the judge**, not grading the system. You cannot afford it at volume, so you spend it establishing whether the cheap thing you *can* run at volume agrees with you — which is 9.12's κ measurement, and it is the only thing that makes rung three trustworthy.

d.title: Deterministic checks measure a contract, not a lesser kind of quality
d.caption: 12.7's migration is the case for this rung. **The quality gate passed on day 10 — task accuracy went 0.86 to 0.88 — while valid-JSON fell to 94.2%**, which is one request in eighteen unparseable. A judge scoring helpfulness cannot see that, because the answer *was* helpful; it simply was not parseable. So these checks are not a beginner's version of evaluation to be outgrown — **they measure whether the output satisfies a contract**, which is a different question from whether it is good.

d.title: Four judge biases, and the one that is a format choice
d.caption: Three of these are controlled by how you run the judge. The fourth is controlled by **what you ask it**: "rate 1–10" is unstable run to run, and **"which is better" is far more stable** — so preferring pairwise is not a refinement, it removes a failure mode rather than mitigating one. Self-preference is the only row where the fix is a different model family, because no instruction removes a model's taste for its own style.

cells.text: prefer pairwise - it removes the mode

d.title: Storing the model inside the prompt artefact is a validity statement
d.caption: **A prompt is fitted to a model the way hyperparameters are fitted to a dataset** — few-shot count and ordering, chain-of-thought scaffolding, output-format instructions, all tuned against one model's quirks. So putting `model:` in the YAML beside the template is not redundant metadata: **it asserts that this template is only valid against that model**, which makes a model change a reason to re-validate the prompt rather than a config edit. The changelog entry does the same job for the reason the rule exists.

nodes.label: A prompt is fitted to a model
So model: belongs in the artefact
And the changelog records why each rule exists

d.title: A -0.02 gate on 100 cases is inside the noise
d.caption: 9.16's arithmetic applies directly: **at a pass rate near 0.90 a 100-case suite carries a 95% margin of about ±4.3 points**, so a gate that blocks a regression beyond −0.02 is blocking on a quantity it cannot measure. A 400-case suite halves that to about ±2.2 and still does not reach it. **The fix is not a different constant** — it is to compare the two runs as a *paired* comparison on the same cases, which removes the example-difficulty variance that dominates the margin.

nodes.label: Pair the runs on the same cases

d.title: Prompt drift needs no deprecation notice
d.caption: This is the quiet version of a forced migration: **the alias moves, the model changes, and a prompt tuned against the old one is now tuned against nothing.** The instruction that follows is simple and widely skipped — **re-run the eval set on every model upgrade**, not because the model got worse but because your prompt was fitted to a different one. And 10.8 measured why you will not notice otherwise: an alias roll is gradual, **19.9% of traffic on day one and 100% on day two**, so a by-day quality chart shows a slope rather than a step.

nodes.label: Re-run the eval set on every upgrade

d.title: Three mechanisms, and the sequencing that follows
d.caption: The decision is about **what you need to change**, and the three answers do not overlap. Facts baked into weights **go stale**, require a training run to update rather than an index write, and **cannot be cited** — the third is the one that surprises people, and 11.1 explains it: the objective rewards plausible continuations, so training on your facts makes plausible-sounding variants of them more likely too. So: prompt first, then RAG for knowledge, then fine-tune for behaviour, format or cost.
cells: nothing in the model; just instructions
our exact JSON schema, house tone

d.title: Every metric the team watched improved
d.caption: Task accuracy went **70% to 92% — up 22 points**, which is the number in the pull request and the number in the summary. The general benchmark went **85% to 61%**, and nobody was watching it. This is the same structure as 11.17's closing rule: **a single number that only improves is measuring one error direction**, and the direction it is not measuring is where the damage went. The fix is to keep a general-ability metric in the gate, not to fine-tune less.

d.title: Two shapes, and the recommendation whose clever half is easy to miss
d.caption: A **pinned snapshot** gives stable, reproducible behaviour and a predictable, scheduled incident — you must migrate on a deadline. A **floating alias** gives no deadline and an unpredictable incident, which is 12.2's prompt drift. The usual advice is to pin, and the second half is the clever part: **run a nightly golden-set eval against the floating alias as well**, so you learn about the next model's behaviour before the deadline forces you onto it.

d.title: Six ways a prompt fails to transfer
d.caption: The second row is the one that costs money rather than quality: **a reasoning model does chain-of-thought natively, so your "think step by step" instruction makes it *over*-think and inflates cost** — the prompt that helped on the old model is actively harmful on the new one. And the last two rows are the silent pair: verbosity that adds 40% length with no quality gain, and a changed system-against-user weighting that destabilises a persona nobody re-tested.

d.title: The real tokenizer spread is 4.9%, not 9.2%
d.caption: The usual illustration is 4,010 against 4,380 tokens — a 9.2% gap. Measured across five tokenizers on the same text the real spread is **4.9%**, narrower than advertised. Which sharpens rather than dismisses the risk: **the danger is less that models differ from each other and more that a context guard calibrated on an optimistic tokens-per-word figure is wrong in the unsafe direction.** t5-small at 1.527 tokens per word and roberta at the top of the range are both plausible assumptions, and only one of them overflows.

d.title: Alert on model_served != model_requested
d.caption: One comparison on two fields, and it catches **silent alias re-points, regional routing differences and provider-side fallbacks** — three things that have no other signature. 10.8 measured why the *requested* field cannot do this job: an alias roll is gradual, **19.9% of traffic on day one and 100% on day two**, so the request field is identical throughout and only the response field moves. Log both, compare them, and the cause arrives named rather than inferred.

d.title: Eight signals, and the two that are incidents rather than thresholds
d.caption: Most of these have a threshold you tune. **Two do not: a `model_served` mismatch and a deprecation header are each an occurrence to act on**, because there is no acceptable rate of being silently moved to a different model. The third row is the one that catches what no deploy explains — a scheduled golden-set eval finds behaviour changes with nothing shipped, which is 12.2's drift made visible.

d.title: A 15% cost alert cannot see a 10% tokenizer change
d.caption: The signal is assigned to catch a tokenizer *or* a pricing change, and **it catches pricing fine, because a price change moves cost directly.** A tokenizer change does not: input tokens are only part of the bill, so a 10% token-count shift moves cost by **7.9% and the 15% alert does not fire.** Even 20% only just trips it. **And this is not a bad threshold** — lowering it to 5% would fire on ordinary traffic-mix variation. The signal simply cannot see this failure, and the thing that can is a per-request token-count monitor.

d.title: Text abstracts easily; tool calls are where the provider differences live
d.caption: **Every provider returns a string, so abstracting text buys almost nothing** — which is why a thin wrapper that only normalises `.text` feels pointless and is. The part that earns its keep is the **normalised tool-call shape**: that is where provider differences actually bite, and where 1.15's warning applies — a layer that hides the names while the behaviours differ is worse than no layer. Normalise the shape, keep the behaviour differences visible, and pin every model ID you found in the inventory.

d.title: Seven gates, and the one with an absolute floor
d.caption: Six gates are expressed **relative to the old model**, which is why 12.7's day-7 baseline step is impossible to recover if skipped. The second row is different and the difference matters: **schema compliance has an absolute floor of 99.5% as well as a relative one**, because a relative gate would have compared 94.2% against the old 99.7% and failed it — but only after someone chose a relative tolerance loose enough to let 94.2% through.

cells.text: at least the old AND at least 99.5% absolute

d.title: Shadow, re-tune, canary — and two rules people skip
d.caption: Shadow first, because replaying production traffic has **zero user risk and catches format breakage immediately**. Then expect real re-tuning work: prompts are model-specific artefacts, not portable config. **Exercise the kill switch at 5%** — a kill switch used for the first time during an incident is a second incident. And **keep both prompt versions live during the canary**, so the old model keeps the prompt it was tuned against rather than running someone else's.

d.title: The timeline, and the day that is impossible to recover
d.caption: Inventory, quota, golden set, baseline, shadow, fix, re-run — **all before a single user request touches the new model.** The inventory alone found 14 hardcoded model IDs across 6 services. **Day 7 is the step easiest to skip and impossible to recover: baseline the old model on the golden set.** Every gate in 12.6 is expressed relative to the old model, so without that baseline there is nothing to compare against and the gates become absolute numbers somebody guessed.

d.title: Accuracy up, latency down, and one request in eighteen unparseable
d.caption: **Every signal a quality-focused suite watches improved**: accuracy up two points, p95 latency down from 1.9 s to 1.4 s. And valid-JSON fell from 99.7% to **94.2% — one request in eighteen**. 12.1 made this the argument for the deterministic rung and 12.6 made it the argument for the contract slice. The absolute floor matters here too: a purely relative gate would have had to compare 94.2% against 99.7% with a tolerance somebody chose, and 99.5% absolute leaves no room for that judgement.

d.title: The fix was three deletions and one setting
d.caption: Day 12's fix adds nothing. **Enable strict schema mode, then delete the now-redundant "respond only in JSON" instruction** and the formatting scaffolding around it — because the new model honours the schema natively and the old instructions were fighting it, producing the code fences that broke the parser. Which is the generalisable lesson of a migration: **a prompt tuned around an old model's weakness becomes a prompt fighting a new model's strength.**

nodes.label: It was working around a weakness

d.title: Checking the verbosity-to-cost claim
d.caption: Verbosity creep is listed as a cost risk, and it is worth putting the arithmetic behind it rather than asserting it. **Output tokens are priced several times input**, so a verbosity change hits the bill harder per token than an input change — but output is usually the smaller share, so the two effects partly cancel. The 20% flag in 12.6's gate table is calibrated on that balance: large enough not to fire on ordinary variation, small enough to catch a model that got chattier.
